original_question: Is it true that a periodic group containing an involution is locally finite if the centralizer of every element of even order is locally finite?

missing_details: To make it fully stand-alone, spell out that "periodic" means every element of the group has finite order; the paper uses the standard term without elaboration here. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
It helps to say explicitly that an "involution" is an element of order 2. The paper leaves this implicit as standard terminology. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))

For complete self-containment, one can write the centralizer as C_G(x) and say the hypothesis is quantified over every element x of G whose order is even. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))

For readers outside the immediate area, one can unpack "locally finite" as meaning that every finitely generated subgroup is finite. The paper states the problem without re-defining the term. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))

There are no additional paper-specific restrictions here: no finiteness assumption beyond periodicity, no solvability assumption, no bound on element orders, and no extra notation or side conditions attached to Problem 21.96. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
refined_question: Let G be a periodic group, i.e. a group in which every element has finite order, and suppose that G contains an involution. If, for every element x in G of even order, the centralizer C_G(x) is locally finite, must G itself be locally finite? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
